title: Tables AND red objects
labels: Expert A alone: tables in different colours
notes: The first expert supplies table shape and several colours.
The second expert supplies red appearance across several shapes.
Most displayed outputs combine red and table shape; one is nearly blank.
All six displayed outputs are recognizable red table-like objects.
The displayed samples are dominated by red tables. This grid does not show the full diversity expected from an OR mixture.
The outputs change to cyan/green table-like shapes, with some distortion and strong saturation.
setup: Two separately trained experts: one on rendered tables in several colours, one on red objects. Their shared preference is a red table.
method: Both AND rows use 0.5sA + 0.5sB, as labelled in the supplied grid. This corresponds to a tempered target proportional to sqrt(pA pB), not the full product used in the Gaussian teaching example.
finding: The annealed ULA row is more consistent in this displayed grid. The naive row already contains red tables, so the result supports a sample-quality comparison rather than an all-or-nothing success claim.
limit: Six displayed samples per row are qualitative evidence. Training budgets, sampler settings, runtime, energy calibration and aggregate metrics were not supplied.

title: Classifier conditioning
notes: Without guidance, the samples do not follow the requested digit columns.
Conditioning largely follows the target labels. Some shapes remain ambiguous, including the displayed target-5 sample.
The displayed row contains readable examples of the requested digits.
The supplied row is labelled Metropolis-adjusted MALA. Relative density or energy information is required to justify its acceptance step.
setup: Requested labels run from 0 to 9. An unconditional digit model is compared with classifier-guided reverse sampling, ULA and a MALA-labelled run.
method: The conditioning rule adds the noisy classifier gradient to the generative score. This is the paper's Section 5.3 / Equation 14 adapted to digits.
finding: Conditioning visibly changes the outputs toward the requested labels. These single examples per target do not establish dataset-wide accuracy or a ranking of ULA and MALA.
limit: The image does not include classifier accuracy, guidance strength for the conditional rows, runtime, acceptance rates or the energy implementation used by MALA.

title: Text-to-image composition
labels: House AND red: naive score combination
House AND red AND NOT trees: latent ULA
notes: Five source columns are labelled seeds 1 through 5.
The red prompt evokes red surfaces, clothing and people rather than a particular object category.
Several baseline samples already combine a house with red. Seed 2 is closer to a wall/window than a full house.
Latent ULA changes detail and scene layout. Several outputs retain both concepts; seed 2 remains door-like.
The scenes change again and several views have little visible vegetation. One output is interior-like, so preserving the desired scene remains a concern.
setup: The supplied experiment uses Stable Diffusion v1.5. Five seed columns compare separate prompts, naive composition, latent ULA and a NOT-trees composition.
method: This is a pretrained text-to-image reuse experiment. The figure alone does not specify prompt weights, guidance settings, a base-score correction or the latent update schedule.
finding: The effect is mixed across seeds. The naive baseline is already strong in several columns, so this grid does not establish a universal advantage for latent ULA.
limit: Prompt alignment scores, full prompt strings, matched compute and sampler logs were not supplied. Display labels below correct the source's stray references to tables; the original image is preserved.
